message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Below is an overview of key rights you typically enjoy as a renter: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights (Texas) | Notes | |----------|------------------------------|-------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Landlords must itemize deductions and provide receipts if requested. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain premises in a safe, sanitary condition; repair structural defects, plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.
• Must keep common areas clean and safe. | If landlord fails, tenants may withhold rent, repair & deduct, or terminate lease. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (usually 24‑hour written notice unless emergency).
• Landlord must respect privacy. | Exceptions: emergencies, repairs, inspections with proper notice. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination: 60 days’ notice for month‑to‑month leases; 90 days for longer leases.
• For rent increase: 30 days’ notice for increases less than 10% of current rent; 90 days for larger increases. | Notice must be in writing and delivered personally or via certified mail. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent due on the day specified in the lease (often the first of the month).
• Late fees allowed but capped at 5% of monthly rent. | Landlord may not demand payment before the due date. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, tenant may pay for repairs and deduct cost from rent (up to $500 per year). | Must give landlord notice and reasonable time to repair. | | **Lease Termination** | • Tenants can terminate early with written notice and may be required to pay a penalty (often one month’s rent).
• Landlord may terminate for cause (e.g., nonpayment, violation of lease). | Both parties must follow notice periods. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected against discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. (under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law). | Landlord cannot refuse or treat differently based on protected class. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment).
• Eviction requires court action; landlord cannot forcibly remove tenant. | Tenants can contest eviction in court. | | **Privacy & Access** | • Landlord must provide reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | Landlord may not enter during “quiet hours” (typically 10 p.m.–7 a.m.). | | **Maintenance of Records** | • Landlord must keep records of rent payments and maintenance requests. | Tenants can request copies. | ### Practical Steps for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – It may contain terms that modify or add to statutory rights. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of notices, emails, photos of damage, and a log of maintenance requests. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Send notices and complaints via certified mail or email so you have proof. 4. **Know When to Seek Legal Help** – If your landlord violates your rights, consider contacting a local tenant advocacy group or attorney. ### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division**: Offers guides and complaint forms. - **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)**: Provides resources on fair housing and landlord‑tenant issues. - **Local Tenant Advocacy Groups**: Many cities have nonprofits that offer free or low‑cost legal assistance. If you’re facing a specific issue (e.g., landlord refusing to make repairs, dispute over security deposit), let me know the details and I can help draft a formal letter or outline next steps.
